newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian business chief calls for state sell-offs.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian business chief calls for state sell-offs.

text.p: The managing director of Nigerian conglomerate UAC called on Nigeria's military rulers to swiftly privatise state-run utilities.
In a statement, Bassey Ndiokho said the petroleum sector, the state-run telephone company NITEL and the power generator NEPA were among those industries that should be privatised as soon as possible.
"The economic well-being of this country hinges largely on the efficiency of these organisations, hence the urgency of the need to privatise them," Ndiokho said.

In his 1997 budget, military strongman General Sani Abacha shied away from quick privatisations but promised that a committee which would look into the possibility and also pledged that state-run bodies would have to operate on a commercial basis.
"The persistent lack of progress in these parastatals is a pointer to the fact that palliative steps such as commercialisation can hardly improve their performance," Ndiokho said.

Crude oil-exporting Nigeria is just emerging from weeks of fuel shortages, only resolved by importing petrol, while telephone and power utilities provide services which are erratic at best, forcing up operating costs for businesses.
Abacha's tight fiscal policies appear to have crushed rampant inflation and stabilised the currency, but have also kept Africa's most populous nation of over 100 million people in recession.

"The pursuit of further reduction in the inflation rate to a 15 percent target level set for 1997 to me is excellent, but the side effects of these measures on the economic well-being of the citizenry should also be taken into consideration," Ndiokho said.

Nigeria's economy is largely dependent on spending proceeds from crude oil exports, which is partly why business and the World Bank were disapointed with the lack of commitment to privatisation, as an alternative for encouraging growth and the inflow of foreign investment.
Ndiokho called for the merging of Nigeria's dual exchange rate, which allows some branches of government access to foreign currency at around a quarter the rate for everyone else.
